reference_calls.source_slice: On 4 November 1922,
in the Valley of the Kings,
labourers engaged by the archaeologist Howard Carter uncovered a staircase carved into the rock.
On 26 November,
with his wealthy sponsor Lord Carnarvon beside him,
Carter made a small hole in the sealed doorway and glimpsed the glittering gold of the boy king Tutankhamun.
Carnarvon sold exclusive rights to The Times,
a monopoly that left competing reporters starved of news.
Within a fortnight,
her words would seem uncanny.
He nicked the bite with a razor while shaving,
it turned septic,
and blood poisoning led to pneumonia.
The 25 exposed to the tomb died at an average age of 70,
versus 75 for the rest,
a margin not statistically significant.
Carnarvon's untimely demise had fuelled the tale,
giving it impetus.
Carter,
the excavator who had unsealed the burial place,
died in March 1939,
aged 64,
almost sixteen years after his patron.
